title: Brainstem Atlas
subtitle: Trace midbrain, pons, medulla, nuclei and ascending systems
altText: Interactive chalkboard-style anatomical atlas of Brainstem with labelled regions and pathway relationships.
learningObjectives: Locate major cranial-nerve and arousal systems.
Recognise clinically urgent patterns associated with brainstem dysfunction.

sections.explainSimply: The brainstem links the brain, spinal cord and cerebellum while regulating breathing, heart rate, sleep, arousal and many cranial-nerve functions.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Brainstem systems shape state regulation, sensory gating and autonomic stability, meaning small lesions can produce broad cognitive, behavioural and medical effects.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The midbrain, pons and medulla contain cranial-nerve nuclei, reticular formation, long ascending and descending tracts, neuromodulatory nuclei and cardiorespiratory centres. Compact anatomy makes focal lesions clinically dense and often crossed in their signs.
sections.thinkOfItLike: It is a compact transport hub and life-support control room: major routes pass through while local stations regulate essential functions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Changes in arousal, eye movements, swallowing, autonomic regulation or crossed sensory-motor signs can indicate urgent brainstem pathology.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Attributing fluctuating consciousness or cranial-nerve changes to anxiety without neurological assessment may delay recognition of serious disease.
sections.clinicalPearl: Brainstem symptoms are often disproportionate to lesion size because many critical pathways are packed into a small space.
sections.practicalExample: A pontine lesion may combine ipsilateral facial weakness with contralateral limb weakness because a cranial-nerve nucleus and corticospinal tract are affected together.
sections.limitationsCautions: New diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria, collapse, respiratory change or altered consciousness warrants urgent medical assessment.

anatomy.label: Midbrain
anatomy.function: Eye movements, orienting, motor modulation and arousal
anatomy.inputs: Cortical, retinal, cerebellar and sensory input
anatomy.outputs: Thalamic, spinal, cerebellar and cranial-motor outputs
anatomy.connections: Cortical, retinal, cerebellar and sensory input; projects via Thalamic, spinal, cerebellar and cranial-motor outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Oculomotor deficits, altered arousal, parkinsonian signs
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess midbrain in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Pons
anatomy.function: Cortico-cerebellar relay, facial sensation and movement, sleep regulation
anatomy.inputs: Cortical, cerebellar, vestibular and sensory input
anatomy.connections: Cortical, cerebellar, vestibular and sensory input; projects via Cerebellar, cranial-motor and long-tract outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Facial weakness, gaze palsy, ataxia, locked-in syndrome
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess pons in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Medulla
anatomy.function: Cardiorespiratory control, swallowing and lower cranial functions
anatomy.inputs: Visceral, spinal, vestibular and cortical input
anatomy.connections: Visceral, spinal, vestibular and cortical input; projects via Autonomic, cranial-motor and spinal outputs.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess medulla in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Reticular formation
anatomy.function: Arousal, attention, sleep-wake regulation and pain modulation
anatomy.outputs: Thalamic, hypothalamic, cortical and spinal outputs
anatomy.connections: Diffuse sensory and cortical input; projects via Thalamic, hypothalamic, cortical and spinal outputs.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess reticular formation in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Long tracts
anatomy.function: Carry motor, somatosensory and autonomic information through the brainstem
anatomy.inputs: Cortex, spinal cord and peripheral sensory systems
anatomy.outputs: Spinal cord, thalamus, cerebellum and cortex
anatomy.connections: Cortex, spinal cord and peripheral sensory systems; projects via Spinal cord, thalamus, cerebellum and cortex.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Weakness, sensory loss, ataxia and crossed signs
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess long tracts in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

pathwayTrace.title: Trace brainstem systems vertically
pathwayTrace.instruction: Follow long tracts and arousal systems across brainstem levels, then compare intact conduction with a focal disruption.

pathways.label: Long-tract transit
pathways.summary: Descending motor and ascending sensory systems traverse compact brainstem corridors while interacting with cranial-nerve nuclei.
pathways.healthy: Long pathways carry information through successive brainstem levels while local nuclei add cranial, autonomic and cerebellar functions.
pathways.disrupted: A focal brainstem lesion can combine ipsilateral cranial-nerve findings with contralateral long-tract deficits, creating crossed neurological signs.

pathways.label: Ascending arousal system
pathways.summary: Diffuse reticular systems project rostrally to thalamic, hypothalamic and cortical arousal networks.
pathways.healthy: Distributed reticular and ascending projections support wakefulness, attention and state regulation.
pathways.disrupted: Bilateral or strategically placed lesions affecting ascending arousal systems can markedly reduce consciousness, but coma localisation requires full neurological and systemic assessment.

lesionLab.title: Brainstem localisation challenge
lesionLab.instruction: Use the combination of cranial, long-tract and arousal findings to choose the best level or system.

cases.label: Case 1
cases.prompt: A focal syndrome combines an ipsilateral cranial-nerve deficit with contralateral limb weakness and sensory change.
cases.rationale: Crossed signs strongly suggest a brainstem localisation where cranial-nerve structures and ascending or descending long tracts lie in close proximity.
cases.caveat: The exact level depends on which cranial nerve and tract modalities are affected; this simplified map is not sufficient for bedside localisation.

cases.label: Case 2
cases.prompt: Following a central brainstem injury, the dominant change is profound reduction in wakefulness without a simple isolated limb syndrome.
cases.rationale: The reticular formation and associated ascending arousal systems are central to wakefulness and state regulation.
cases.caveat: Reduced consciousness has many structural, metabolic, toxic and epileptic causes and always requires urgent comprehensive assessment.

clinicalComparison.title: Compare intact brainstem pathways with focal disruption
clinicalComparison.instruction: Link compact anatomy to the combination of cranial-nerve, long-tract, arousal and autonomic findings.

comparisons.label: Long-tract integrity

healthy.label: Continuous ascending and descending pathways
healthy.summary: Major motor and sensory tracts traverse the brainstem while maintaining organised transmission.
healthy.mechanism: Long fibres connect spinal, brainstem, thalamic and cortical levels.
healthy.observable: Motor and sensory function is consistent with intact tract conduction.

pathology.label: Focal long-tract interruption
pathology.summary: A compact lesion can affect descending motor or ascending sensory fibres together with nearby cranial-nerve systems.
pathology.mechanism: Dense tract packing allows a small lesion to disrupt multiple neighbouring pathways.
pathology.observable: Crossed or combined cranial-nerve and contralateral long-tract signs may appear.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: The combination of signs is usually more localising than any single symptom.
comparisons.assessment: Map side, modality and cranial-nerve involvement; abrupt onset or reduced consciousness requires urgent medical evaluation.
comparisons.caveat: Brainstem syndromes vary with lesion level, extent and vascular anatomy and are not reliably diagnosed from symptoms alone.

comparisons.label: Arousal systems

healthy.label: Sustained arousal regulation
healthy.summary: Brainstem arousal systems support wakefulness and modulate cortical state through widespread projections.
healthy.mechanism: Reticular and neuromodulatory systems interact with thalamic, hypothalamic and cortical targets.
healthy.observable: Wakefulness is maintained appropriately for sleep-wake state and context.

pathology.label: Arousal-system disruption
pathology.summary: Bilateral or strategically placed dysfunction can impair alertness and consciousness.
pathology.mechanism: Damage to ascending arousal pathways reduces effective activation of distributed forebrain systems.
pathology.observable: Somnolence, reduced alertness or more severe impairment of consciousness may occur.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: Altered consciousness is a medical sign with a broad differential; localisation is only one part of the assessment.
comparisons.assessment: Prioritise acute medical assessment, neurological examination and physiological causes before neuropsychological interpretation.
comparisons.caveat: Sedation, metabolic disturbance, seizure, sleep loss and diffuse brain dysfunction can also alter arousal.

assessmentLab.title: Assessment-linked brainstem reasoning
assessmentLab.instruction: Choose the most informative first assessment domain, then compare findings that would strengthen or weaken the localisation hypothesis.

cases.label: Long-tract pattern
cases.prompt: A patient develops new unilateral weakness with altered sensation and brisk reflexes after an acute neurological event. Which domain should be prioritised first?
cases.rationale: A long-tract hypothesis is tested most directly by the pattern of weakness, tone, reflexes, sensory change and side-to-side relationships before higher-order cognitive testing.
observe: sensory level or crossed sensory findings
supports: convergent cranial nerve or long-tract signs
challenges: a pattern better explained by peripheral nerve, neuromuscular or musculoskeletal pathology
absence of neurological signs despite a stable severe complaint
cases.nextStep: Escalate urgently for acute or progressive focal neurological signs; neuropsychological testing is secondary to medical localisation and stabilisation.
cases.caveat: Long-tract signs localise a system, not necessarily a single lesion. Brain, brainstem, spinal cord and mixed pathologies can produce overlapping patterns.

cases.label: Arousal / reticular pattern
cases.prompt: A patient is unusually difficult to rouse and shows fluctuating attention. What should come before formal cognitive testing?
cases.rationale: Reduced or fluctuating arousal can invalidate downstream cognitive testing and may signal an acute medical or neurological problem.
taskTypes: brief attention probes only when sufficiently alert
supports: temporal association with acute illness or medication change
challenges: stable alertness with selectively impaired cognition
a longstanding developmental attentional profile without altered consciousness
cases.nextStep: Treat altered consciousness as a medical assessment problem first; defer extensive neuropsychological testing until arousal is sufficiently stable.
cases.caveat: Arousal disturbance is highly non-specific and can arise from structural, metabolic, toxic, infectious, sleep-related and psychiatric causes.
